21 October 2026: condominium linkage correction in progress

Update, 22 October: Dataset 1.2.0 has now been released. The account below records the position on 21 October.

The earlier Bronx story attributed a large linkage gap to public-record coverage. My code searched condo unit lots only through 1999; the city documents unit lots through 6999. That coding restriction explains much of the gap. The story's original interpretation is withdrawn.

Condominium deed links and mortgage searches, the dataset tables, and condo results in the Tax and House papers are being checked. The explorer temporarily suppresses affected link statistics, while retaining raw counts and price medians. Condo graphics are withdrawn from active press downloads. New paper results and a corrected dataset have not yet been released.

The Deed paper's main index uses a separate deed-level input; no numerical change to it has been demonstrated from this bug. Existing paper PDFs, deposited versions and historical chart archives remain available as dated releases.

The family-transfer story also now describes the checked property as mixed use and removes unsupported claims about marketing or the parties' motives. No new interviews or human audit readings are claimed.

Updates and corrections

Changes to the stories, research links and tools, with a way to report an error.

22 October 2026 · Dataset

Corrected condominium links released

Dataset 1.2.0 expands the unit-lot search from 1999 to 6999. Condominium deed coverage rises from 89.8% to 96.0% citywide and from 51.7% to 98.8% in the Bronx. The sales extract and house-link rows are unchanged. The data page, examples and explorer now use the corrected release. Coverage and field agreement do not establish accuracy against verified documents.

The earlier interpretation of the Bronx gap as missing public records is withdrawn. The House and Tax paper corrections remain separate local drafts pending release.

20 October 2026 · Data explorer and video overview

Explorer updated to dataset 1.1.0, and a verified overview video

The interactive explorer and its aggregate downloads now use dataset version 1.1.0, matching the condominium deed-linkage coverage in the data note and stories (89.8% overall; 96.1% in Brooklyn, 89.7% in Queens, 88.4% in Manhattan and 51.7% in the Bronx). Added How the studies connect on the homepage with verified charts from the papers.

18 October 2026 · New story

Four ways New York could make a first home cheaper to buy

Published a story that brings together the mortgage recording tax, the transfer-tax cliffs, the cash-buyer discount and the gaps in the city’s sales data, with the changes the research points to. No paper result changed.

17 October 2026 · Research links and data description

PolicySpace2 audit files, and what a deed link means

The PolicySpace2 audit behind the reach comparison in When the Benchmark Moves with the Policy is now public: the instrumentation patch, analysis script and per-seed results are in version 1.0.3 of the benchmark audit. No result changed.

The dataset page now says “deed link” where it said “unique deed”. A link requires a single candidate parcel; when several qualifying deeds sit on that parcel, the code keeps the lowest document identifier, which happens for 916 of 297,252 links. Coverage figures are unchanged. The data guide now says that its commands reproduce data release 1.0, and how to get the 1.1.0 coverage table. The tax paper’s citation box now gives the version 3.2 DOI.

The Bronx condominium story now uses dataset 1.1.0. The new condominium rules link more sales in every borough: 96.1% in Brooklyn, 89.7% in Queens, 88.4% in Manhattan and 51.7% in the Bronx, against 74.6%, 65.4%, 78.9% and 44.7% in release 1.0.1. The Bronx gap remains, including within the same price range, so the headline now says the records lose track of half the Bronx’s condominium sales. Charts, tables and CSVs are regenerated.

16 October 2026 · Paper releases and new story

New paper versions, dataset 1.1.0, and a family-sale story

Published new versions across the research program on Zenodo: Who Gets the House? v3.9 (including author verification of all 60 transfer-report readings), The Shape of the Tax v3.2 (adding New Jersey 2004 fee comparison), When a Deed Is Not a Market Sale v1.0.11 (adding Philadelphia sheriff-deed contrast), When the Benchmark Moves with the Policy v7.0 (retitled and merged with the benchmark note), the benchmark audit note v1.0.2, and NYC linked sales dataset v1.1.0 with condominium deed coverage increased to 89.8% (51.7% in the Bronx).

Current papers and a guide to trying the data

Updated the paper downloads and fixed-version citations after a literature and interpretation review. Tax is 3.1, House 3.8, Deed 1.0.10, Wedge 6.5 and the benchmark note 1.0.1; dataset documentation is 1.0.3. Estimates and chart series are unchanged. 14 October 2026 · Research tools and correction

Matched simulation comparisons and current tax-story figures

The simulation explorer compares archived model results under five assumption sets. Its population and benchmark controls keep instrument settings fixed. CSV downloads include units and paired Monte Carlo standard errors. The model remains illustrative.

The tax story and homepage retained older figures after the paper page was updated. They now use preprint v3.0, with one row per deed. The $2 million density ratio after the reform changes from 1.6 to 2.3; the $3 million ratio changes from 1.5 to 2.5. Comparison-price ratios and the $1,999,999 count are updated too: 127 post-reform deeds replaces 131 sales rows. The graphic and CSV match the current paper. A dated graphics pack carries these updates; the original pack remains archived.

The Wedge primary download and benchmark figure now use the verified v6.4 release of 14 October (Zenodo 23362696). The main case uses NYC proxies; the earlier high-competition calibration is a stress test. The explorer retains default-policy runs that this release reuses unchanged and keeps separately tuned target experiments in the paper.

The four paper introductions now give a short finding and its limits. The house page links its existing shared-address sensitivity to the interpretation. The research map includes all three empirical studies and distinguishes the separate simulation. Paper PDFs and published research inputs are unchanged.

13 October 2026 · Research links and site

The Shape of the Tax, v3.0, and a Press page

The Shape of the Tax, v3.0, counts one row per deed and checks the merged rows against the deed registry. The share of sales at exactly $2, $3 or $5 million fell by about 60%, for tax jumps from $5,000 to $37,500 alike, and the result holds against never-taxed prices as round as the thresholds. The paper page's figures are updated: sales at exactly $2 million fell from 7.8 to 2.3 times the local density, and the avoided tax is $1.6–2.9 million a year, under 1% of what the reform's schedule implies.

“For journalists” is now Press, and it opens with the Housing Notes guest post. Footers fit on one line.

13 October 2026 · Research links and a correction

The Shape of the Tax, v2.9, and a correction

The Shape of the Tax, v2.9, is retitled Round Prices and Bunching at New York City's 2019 Transfer-Tax Notches. About 60% of the sales that had closed at exactly $2, $3 or $5 million now close a few thousand dollars below the threshold, by less than the tax saved, whatever the size of the tax jump.

Correction: the 10 October entry below repeated the v2.8 statement that at $2 million prices fell by more than three times the tax saved. That reading assumed a smooth distribution of prices and is withdrawn. Counted directly, the moved sales sit about $2,400 below $2 million. The paper page's figures for the emptied price range and the avoided tax are replaced: the avoided tax is $1.3–2.7 million a year, under 1% of what the reform's schedule implies. The story chart is unchanged.

10 October 2026 · Research links

New paper versions

  • The Shape of the Tax, v2.8: converts the bunching into local incidence and recorded-price elasticities. At $2 million prices fell by more than three times the tax saved, but the implied elasticities are small and local. Mortgage amounts also bunch below the recording tax's own $500,000 loan threshold. Earlier estimates and the story chart are unchanged.
  • Who Gets the House?, v3.7: compares the results with estimates that use commercial data vendors' flags to remove family transfers. No estimate changes.

9 October 2026 · Research links

Current releases and their qualifications

  • Who Gets the House?, v3.6: resolved the deed cross-reference as a power of attorney. In a new sample of 40 sale endpoints, correcting two missed mortgages moves the headline contrast from 9.25 to 9.23 log points in a sensitivity check. Eighteen cases remain unresolved; the check does not establish a population error rate. The published headline and story chart remain unchanged.
  • The Shape of the Tax, v2.7: adds transaction counts and composition checks around the reform. Those comparisons remain descriptive. The story’s threshold chart series are unchanged.
  • When a Deed Is Not a Market Sale, v1.0.9: includes the hedonic comparison and clarifies the interpretation of the index differences. The story’s earlier chart series are retained and identified in its source notes.
  • Dataset documentation, v1.0.2: the underlying data release remains v1.0. Coverage, agreement with earlier code and accuracy against verified documents are distinct measures.

Each paper page links to its fixed archive. Earlier PDF URLs remain available for existing citations.

9 October 2026 · Site and tools

Custom domain, data explorer and mobile layouts

The site now uses nychousingdata.com. The explorer offers filters and downloads from frozen aggregate data; it is not a live market feed. The record guide explains deed amounts and mortgage matches. The tax-threshold illustration covers historical 2019 buyer taxes, with exclusions shown beside the calculation.

Pages use responsive gutters, charts and labelled mobile tables. Press resources collects downloads separately from the full stories.

Report a correction

Email loschi.pablo@gmail.com with the page URL, the passage or figure and a source that helps check it. Please avoid including private identifying details from a transaction.

Substantive corrections will describe the original claim, what changed and which pages are affected. Changes to research findings will link to the revised paper or data release. Routine spelling and layout fixes may be grouped in a site update.
